clinicalPearls: Caused by recessive loss-of-function variants in DYSF encoding dysferlin, a sarcolemmal membrane-repair protein; the same gene underlies Miyoshi myopathy, and the two phenotypes may coexist within one family.
Onset is typically in late adolescence or early adulthood in a previously athletic individual, and many patients recall excellent prior sporting ability before insidious weakness begins.
Two overlapping patterns are recognised: proximal pelvic-girdle weakness (the LGMD R2 pattern) and distal posterior-calf wasting with difficulty standing on tiptoe (the Miyoshi pattern).
Serum creatine kinase is characteristically very markedly elevated, often to a degree that can be mistaken for polymyositis and prompt inappropriate immunosuppression.
Muscle imaging often shows early selective involvement of the gastrocnemius and soleus with relative sparing until later of more proximal groups, aiding differentiation from sarcoglycanopathies.
Inflammatory infiltrates on biopsy are common and can lead to a mistaken diagnosis of idiopathic inflammatory myopathy; absent dysferlin on immunolabelling redirects the diagnosis.
Cardiac involvement is generally mild or absent, distinguishing dysferlinopathy from the sarcoglycanopathies and from LGMD R9 (FKRP-related).
reference.pathophysiology: LGMD R2 results from biallelic pathogenic variants in DYSF on chromosome 2p13, which encodes dysferlin, a large type II transmembrane protein enriched at the sarcolemma and in T-tubules. Dysferlin is central to calcium-dependent resealing of membrane wounds: when the sarcolemma is torn during contraction, dysferlin coordinates the recruitment and fusion of intracellular repair vesicles to patch the defect. Loss of functional dysferlin leaves myofibres unable to reseal microtears, producing progressive membrane leakage, secondary inflammatory activation, fibre necrosis and regeneration, and eventual fibro-fatty replacement. Because the same gene defect can present as either proximal (limb-girdle) or distal (Miyoshi) weakness, the disorder is best conceptualised as a single dysferlinopathy spectrum. The prominent secondary inflammation explains both the very high creatine kinase and the frequent misclassification as an acquired inflammatory myopathy.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy (polymyositis) given inflammatory biopsy and very high creatine kinase
Anoctaminopathy / LGMD R12 (ANO5), which also causes calf-predominant weakness with high creatine kinase
Sarcoglycanopathies (LGMD R3-R6) with more prominent cardiac and childhood involvement
LGMD R9 (FKRP-related) with calf hypertrophy and cardiorespiratory disease
Calpainopathy / LGMD R1 with scapular winging and contractures
additionalInvestigations: Serum creatine kinase (characteristically very high, especially early)
Muscle MRI of thighs and calves to define the posterior-compartment predominant pattern
Muscle biopsy with immunohistochemistry and immunoblot for dysferlin (reduced or absent)
Monocyte dysferlin assay by flow cytometry as an accessible screening test
Targeted DYSF sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis or a multigene LGMD panel
Electromyography to confirm a myopathic pattern and exclude neurogenic mimics
redFlags: Progressive loss of ability to walk on tiptoe or climb stairs signalling advancing posterior-compartment involvement
Erroneous immunosuppressive treatment for presumed inflammatory myopathy without genetic confirmation
Rapid functional decline after unaccustomed intense exercise
New exertional dyspnoea or reduced exercise tolerance prompting respiratory assessment
reference.prognosis: Progression is variable but generally slow, with many patients remaining ambulant for a long period after onset before pelvic-girdle weakness eventually threatens independent walking. Life expectancy is usually near normal because significant cardiac and respiratory failure are uncommon compared with other subtypes.
pitfalls: Labelling the disorder polymyositis on the basis of inflammatory infiltrate and very high creatine kinase and starting steroids
Assuming a limb-girdle presentation excludes the allelic distal Miyoshi phenotype within the same family
Expecting the marked cardiomyopathy typical of sarcoglycanopathies, which is not a feature here
Relying on a single normal proximal-muscle biopsy when the process is patchy and posterior-calf predominant
references: Peer-reviewed limb-girdle muscular dystrophy classification and consensus statements
management: No disease-modifying drug therapy exists; a key management step is to avoid the corticosteroids/immunosuppression often given when the markedly raised creatine kinase and inflammatory biopsy are mistaken for polymyositis, as these do not help and may worsen dysferlinopathy
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy to preserve range of movement, prevent contractures and provide orthoses and mobility aids as weakness progresses
Guidance to avoid strenuous eccentric and high-impact exercise that provokes sarcolemmal microtears, with low-impact activity and weight management encouraged
Periodic respiratory surveillance with erect and supine spirometry, introducing non-invasive ventilation if respiratory muscle weakness emerges
Baseline and periodic cardiac assessment with ECG and echocardiography, though clinically significant cardiac involvement is uncommon in this subtype
Multidisciplinary neuromuscular clinic care with orthopaedic and spinal input for contracture and posture management
Genetic counselling and carrier testing for relatives given autosomal recessive inheritance, noting the shared DYSF basis with Miyoshi myopathy
